d.title: Three assumptions at the top, and every rule below is derived
d.caption: **Nothing on the lower level is an extra assumption** — each one follows from the three above it, which is worth seeing once so the rules stop feeling like a list to memorise. The word *disjoint* in the third axiom is the important one: **it is exactly why the union rule has to subtract the overlap.** Add two overlapping events and the shared part is counted twice. And “equally likely” is nowhere on this diagram, because it is a property of the sample space you chose, not a law.

d.title: Why 23 people is a coin flip, and 253 is the number to look at
d.caption: **The middle column is the entire explanation.** People picture “someone shares *my* birthday”, which needs about 253 people for even odds. The question actually asked is about *any* pair — and 23 people make 253 pairs, each with a 1-in-365 chance. **The same 253 appearing in both places is not a coincidence.** The engineering form is the one to carry: a collision becomes likely after roughly the square root of N draws, not N/2, which is why a 256-bit hash offers about 128 bits of collision resistance.

d.title: One experiment, three random variables, three different distributions
d.caption: **A random variable is a function, and that is the whole point of the definition.** The 36 outcomes of two dice are fixed; what varies is which numeric question you ask of them. The sum, the larger die and “did they match” are three different functions on the *same* sample space, so each has its own distribution — obtained by pushing the probabilities on the outcomes through the function. **The randomness is in which outcome occurs; the function itself is a deterministic rule**, which is why X is written with a capital and the value it took is written small.

nodes.label: Three distributions
nodes.sub: each is the pushforward of one function

d.title: The same question, asked two ways, in the tail
d.caption: **At 115 the two routes agree, and at 230 one of them has nothing left to give.** float64 holds about 16 digits, so once the CDF exceeds 1 minus 1e-16 it rounds to exactly 1.0 and the subtraction returns zero — **not a small number, zero.** The survival function computes the tail directly and never does that subtraction, which is why libraries ship `sf` as a separate function rather than as a convenience. It is the same cancellation that makes E[X²] − E[X]² a bad way to compute a variance.

d.title: Three answers you could not get any other way
d.caption: **In every row the pieces are strongly dependent, and in every row it does not matter** — linearity of expectation needs no independence and no knowledge of the joint distribution at all. The recipe is always the same: write the count as a sum of indicators, use the fact that the expectation of an indicator *is* a probability, and add. **Row one is the one to remember: shuffle a million hats and the expected number of people getting their own back is exactly 1.** Simulated at n = 1,000 it comes out at 1.002.

steps.code: n keys into N hash buckets

d.title: Add two variables and the variance depends on whether they move together
d.caption: **Both rows have the same two variances; only the correlation differs, and the answer is 90% larger.** Var(X+Y) is Var(X) + Var(Y) + twice the covariance, and dropping that cross term is one of the more expensive habits in applied work — it is exactly how a portfolio, a latency budget or an error budget gets reported as safer than it is. **The scaling row is the other half: doubling a quantity quadruples its variance** while the standard deviation merely doubles, which is why the standard deviation is the one that belongs in a report.

d.title: Having waited five minutes changes nothing, which is often the wrong model
d.caption: **The two numbers are identical, and that is the property.** “I have waited 5 minutes, what is the chance of another 10” equals “the chance of 10 from a standing start” — the clock resets continuously, and the exponential is the only continuous distribution that does this. **Which makes it exactly right for a process with no internal state and badly wrong for anything that ages.** If a long-running request is *less* likely to finish soon, the hazard rate is rising, and a timeout is the correct response rather than more patience.

state: no notion of age at all

d.title: One shape parameter, and the mode leaves zero
d.caption: **At k = 1 the Gamma *is* the exponential** — same distribution, mode sitting at zero. Raise k and the mode moves out to (k−1) times the scale, because waiting for the third event is not like waiting for the first. **That is the modelling signal worth taking from this table: if your latency histogram rises to a peak and then falls, an exponential cannot fit it**, since its mode is always at zero. Reach for a Gamma rather than transforming the data until the exponential looks acceptable. At large k it approaches a normal — the CLT arriving, since this is a sum of k exponentials.

d.title: Conditioning throws rows away and rescales what is left
d.caption: **Learning something does not change the relative sizes inside the condition — only the denominator.** Start from a joint table where 19.5% of all users churned. Condition on paid and you keep one row, divide by 0.300, and get 5%. Condition on churned instead and you divide by 0.195 to get 7.7%. **Same cell on top, different denominators, and that is the whole reason P(A given B) and P(B given A) are different numbers** — the mistake behind every misread medical test and every confused churn dashboard.

d.title: A common cause and a common effect pull in opposite directions
d.caption: **These are the two shapes behind “should I control for this variable?”, and they answer it oppositely** — which is why “control for everything” is unsafe advice rather than cautious advice. Ice cream and drownings correlate at 0.771 because both follow temperature; hold the temperature in a narrow band and the correlation falls to 0.011. **A collider does the reverse: conditioning on a common effect manufactures an association between causes that were genuinely unrelated.** Independence and conditional independence are different properties, and neither implies the other.

d.title: Everything comes out of the joint table, and nothing goes back in
d.caption: **One direction works and the other does not, which is the point of the section.** Sum the joint over a variable and you have a marginal; divide by a marginal and you have a conditional. **But the marginals cannot rebuild the joint** — many different joint tables share the same row and column totals, and everything about how the two variables relate lives in that gap. Which is also where the tests live: **chi-square and mutual information both measure the distance between the observed joint and the product of the marginals.**

d.title: Drop the off-diagonal and the risk comes out a third too low
d.caption: **Three things, two of which share a driver — and the naive sum of weighted variances understates the real spread by nearly half.** The correct expression is w-transpose Sigma w: one line, every covariance included, always right. The shortcut of summing w-squared times sigma-squared quietly assumes every off-diagonal entry is zero, **which is false for anything with a common cause: two services behind one database, two features derived from one measurement, two assets in one sector.** The same off-diagonal information is what makes a minimum-variance portfolio possible at all.

d.title: Surprise, in bits, and why it has to be a logarithm
d.caption: **Three requirements pin the formula down completely:** a certain event must not be surprising, a rarer event must be more surprising, and independent surprises must add. **Only the logarithm satisfies all three** — so surprise is minus log p, and entropy is just its average. The unit is real rather than decorative: one bit is exactly a fair coin flip, and the entropy of a distribution is a hard lower bound on the average bits per symbol that any encoder can reach. **It is a compression limit, not an index.**

state: a fair coin flip: one bit

steps.code: average it over a fair coin

d.title: Zero bits, one bit, and the quarter-bit in between
d.caption: **Mutual information is the gap from the previous lesson, measured in bits** — the KL divergence between the joint table and the product of its marginals. It is zero exactly when the variables are independent, and it reaches one full bit when Y is a copy of X, because knowing Y then removes a whole bit of uncertainty. **Unlike correlation it catches any dependence at all, linear or not.** The caution is the last row: two features can each score highly against the target and be duplicates of one another, so ranking features one at a time selects the same information twice.

d.title: The same question, two bounds, fourteen orders of magnitude apart
d.caption: **Ten thousand requests at a 1% error rate: can the error count double to 200?** Hoeffding knows only that each indicator lies between 0 and 1, so it must allow for a distribution piled at the ends, and returns a useless 0.27. Chernoff knows the mean is 100 and that doubling it takes a conspiracy, and returns 3e-15. **When your variables are indicators — a click, a failure, a cache hit — using Hoeffding leaves nearly all of the information on the table.** The multiplicative form is why: the bound scales with the mean rather than with the range.
